full_text:
More than 900 academics have voiced their opposition to the government’s decision to block the climate academic Andreas Malm from entering the UK, warning that the move represents “a grave violation of academic freedom and freedom of expression”.

Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline and a leading climate scholar, was prevented from entering the UK last week by the Home Office after being told that his presence in the UK “may not be considered to be conducive to the public good”.

He had been due to attend an academic conference on Wednesday, appear on the BBC, and participate in a public discussion organised by the publication Tribune alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed organisation Palestine Action.

Hundreds of academics have signed an open letter voicing their concern at the move and calling on the government to overturn the decision.

“The ability of scholars to travel, exchange ideas and participate in public debate – including on politically contentious issues – is fundamental to a free and democratic society,” the letter says. “Excluding academics because of their political views or the topics they discuss sets a dangerous precedent and risks creating a chilling effect on academic and public discourse.”

Malm, an associate professor at Lund University in Sweden and an internationally recognised climate academic, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked, but said he suspected it was because of his plans to appear on a panel alongside Ammori from Palestine Action.

Speaking to the BBC earlier this week, he said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”

He said the move was “just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Cancelling or refusing an ETA can take place for a range of reasons, including where there are concerns that an individual poses a threat to public safety or seeks to spread extremism.

“It is not a ban on coming to the UK. Those in this position can still apply for a visa, enabling further consideration of circumstances and suitability for entry to the UK.”

The letter has so far been signed by more than 1,400 individuals from over 250 academic institutions, including some of the world’s leading universities.

Fabian Dablander, an assistant professor at the London School of Economics, who initiated the letter, said the numbers showed the strength of feeling in the academic community.

“The letter quickly attracted hundreds of signatures, reflecting the academic community’s deep concern about the threat this decision poses to academic freedom and the UK’s reputation as a place for open intellectual debate,” he said.

title: 5 Takeaways From Democrats’ Historic Night
summary:
5 Takeaways From Democrats’ Historic Night Katherine Knott Wed, 11/04/2026 - 07:07 PM The election results will likely reshape the balance of power in the U.S. for years to come. Higher ed advocates are hopeful that the new Congress will advance their priorities, from college affordability to academic freedom. Here’s what to know so far. Byline(s) IHE Staff 5 Takeaways From Democrats’ Historic Night
Katherine Knott Wed, 11/04/2026 - 07:07 PM

The election results will likely reshape the balance of power in the U.S. for years to come. Higher ed advocates are hopeful that the new Congress will advance their priorities, from college affordability to academic freedom. Here’s what to know so far.

Byline(s)
IHE Staff
full_text:
Tuesday’s election and the “blue tsunami” that followed showed that Americans—particularly young adults and the college-educated—are unsatisfied with the Trump administration’s leadership, and the results will likely resonate for years.

Voters aged 18 to 29 were critical in propelling the Democrats to victory in the House, Senate and a number of state gubernatorial races, with 70 percent voting Democratic, according to The New York Times. That’s a 17-point jump from 2024. Black, Latino and college-educated voters were also key in Democrats’ success.

Not all races in the House and Senate have been called, but as of Wednesday evening, Democrats held a 54-to-44 majority in the Senate and a 237-to-147 majority in the House. The liberals also flipped key governors’ mansions including in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, and broke Republican supermajorities in a number of state legislatures. Experts say the results so far represent a seismic, generational shift in power.

For higher ed, the results of the state and national elections offer a boost to advocates who want to see Democrats rein in the Trump administration and work to make college more affordable without driving students into the private lending market. Now, they’ll be watching closely to see how Democrats deliver on their campaign promises.

Here are Inside Higher Ed’s five takeaways from the historic night.

1. Influential Lawmakers on Higher Ed Knocked Out

When the Democrats swept Congress Tuesday night, they unseated several key leaders of Republican higher ed policy. Chief among them: Susan Collins of Maine, who currently serves as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

During Collins’s three decades in the Senate, she often served as a moderate voice for higher ed and a champion of low-income and first-generation students, protecting programs such as TRIO and the Pell Grant from budget cuts. She also sided with Democrats in multiple attempts to block Trump from redirecting congressional funds and using interagency agreements to hand off the responsibilities of certain education offices.

Her successor, former state legislator Troy Jackson, has criticized the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle the Education Department, as well as Collins’s “failures” to increase education funding in Maine. On the campaign trail, he also vowed to tackle college affordability.

But perhaps no defeat would be more jarring to the Republicans’ higher ed juggernaut than that of Rep. Virginia Foxx, who appeared poised to lose her North Carolina House seat to Democrat Chuck Hubbard. As of Wednesday night, she was down by 99 votes, though Foxx said not all the votes have been counted yet.

Foxx was first elected to the House in 2004 and served as either chair or ranking member of the House education committee from 2017 to 2025. As chair, she grilled college presidents in contentious antisemitism hearings, issued the panel’s first subpoena to a college or university and helped lay the groundwork for a sweeping student loan overhaul. Foxx also has been the primary barrier to the passage of bipartisan legislation that would lift a federal ban on centralized student-level data and modernize the way higher education outcomes are tracked.

Passing the College Transparency Act “is not something that’s going to happen overnight, but it could shift over the course of the next decade … because of an increased reliance on outcomes information to hold institutions accountable,” said Beth Akers, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank.

Even before election night, Senate Republicans had lost the chair of the health and education committee. Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost his re-election bid in the spring after President Trump endorsed his primary competitor, Rep. Julia Letlow. Cassidy was one of seven Republicans who voted to convict Trump following his impeachment over inciting the Jan. 6 insurrection, and as a medical doctor, he also clashed with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over vaccine policies, although he did vote to confirm Kennedy.

Still, Akers and other experts say the exits of Cassidy and other key higher education leaders, particularly after Republicans passed a sweeping higher ed bill in the last Congress, will force the party to redefine its legislative goals involving colleges and universities moving forward.

“Historically Republicans haven’t taken a prominent seat at the higher education policy table … so it’ll be interesting for me to see if they retreat from the issue or if they stay as engaged,” Akers said.

—Jessica Blake

2. Power Shifts in States

For years, Republicans have faced little resistance in their efforts to reshape public higher ed as they passed laws that reduced tenure protections, mandated curriculum reviews, added new general education requirements and banned diversity, equity and inclusion programs, among other changes.

In dozens of states, Republicans either held enough seats in the statehouse to override a governor’s veto or had a trifecta, meaning the party controlled the Legislature and the governor’s mansion. But Democrats broke Republicans’ hold on a number of statehouses on Tuesday night—a shift that could affect who runs universities, since governors and lawmakers often appoint board members, in addition to how those universities are funded and the level of state involvement in their operations.

Democrats flipped the governors’ mansions and broke trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas; in the latter three states, Republicans have advanced significant higher ed policy changes in recent years. And Democrats gained power in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, where they established their own trifectas, according to the National Council for State Legislatures.

“Wisconsin is a huge opportunity,” said Todd Wolfson, president of the American Association of University Professors. “This is the first time that we’ve had an opportunity to overthrow Proposition 10 and regain our collective bargaining rights for faculty across Wisconsin. In Colorado, the last governor, who was a Democrat, vetoed collective bargaining rights for public sector workers, but the incoming governor has signaled that he wants [to change] that. And also in Arizona the state has turned blue, and so there’s huge opportunities around higher education right now.”

Left-leaning lawmakers also gained new footholds in Florida, Kansas and North Carolina, where they broke Republicans’ supermajorities. Over all, Democrats flipped 12 chambers and now lead at least 28 states, up from 15 in 2017. Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams called the results “a massive shift in the landscape of power” that puts the party in its “strongest position in two decades.”

—Katherine Knott

3. AAUP-Endorsed Candidates Win Big

For the first time in its history, the American Association of University Professors endorsed political candidates this election cycle, throwing its weight behind a dozen Democrats in Florida, Michigan, New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania. As part of Tuesday’s “blue tsunami,” 11 of those 12 candidates won their races.

Abdul El-Sayed, AAUP’s first endorsement, became Michigan’s senator-elect, defeating Republican challenger Mike Rogers. Wolfson said his victory “vindicates” the AAUP’s decision to endorse candidates, a move that received blowback from critics and some members.

“We took a lot of crap for that endorsement,” Wolfson said. “But [El-Sayed] has been talking about higher education on the campaign trail in a way that’s really strong.”

AAUP-endorsed Sherrod Brown, a former U.S. senator from Ohio who lost his seat in 2024 and was seeking a fourth term, also notched a victory Tuesday, defeating incumbent Republican Jon Husted. The AAUP backed nine Democrats for House seats, and all nine won their races Tuesday.

Florida state representative and Democratic Socialist Angie Nixon, who ran for U.S. Senate, was the only AAUP-approved candidate to lose her race, conceding Tuesday night to incumbent Republican Ashley Moody. Still, Wolfson remains optimistic about possible progress in Florida and other historically red states.

As for whether the AAUP will continue its endorsements, Wolfson said, “There’s absolutely going to be more next cycle. I can guarantee it.”

—Emma Whitford

4. Trans Athlete Bans Advance

Voters across seven states weighed ballot measures that included a range of proposals, from restricting diversity, equity and inclusion programs and transgender athletes’ participation on teams to allocating billions of dollars to fund academic research and campus construction.

On a night seen as a rebuke of President Trump, who has worked to roll back the rights of trans Americans, voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved new prohibitions on transgender students that bar them from playing on the college sports team that aligns with their gender identity. The Arizona ballot question would also add new restrictions on access to bathrooms and locker rooms A similar measure in Colorado appears likely to pass, though it hadn’t been called as of press time.

But Arizona rejected restrictions on DEI that would have prohibited universities from requiring diversity statements and other measures. Contrastingly, Wisconsin voted to amend the state Constitution to bar preferential treatment based on race, sex, ethnicity and other characteristics. The amendment will apply to public institutions.

Voters also approved higher education funding measures in Rhode Island and New Mexico. Rhode Island voters approved $275 million in bonds for campus construction and renovation projects, while New Mexico signed off on $352 million in bonds for higher education projects.

New Mexico voters also approved changes to how regents are nominated and appointed. While regents were previously tapped by the governor, the passage of Constitutional Amendment 3 will establish nominating committees to advance board picks for gubernatorial approval. The governor will still appoint regents, but she no longer has the same authority to make unilateral picks.

Two funding initiatives were also on the ballot in California. Voters approved Proposition 3, which permanently extends a tax increase on top earners to fund K–12 schools and community colleges. Results for Proposition 38—which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to support immunology research—have not yet been finalized, but it appears likely to pass.

—Josh Moody

5. Results Give Hope to Higher Ed Advocates

Higher education advocates are hopeful that more Democrats in office next year will mean more support for colleges and universities.

“The midterm election results are a clear call to make college more affordable and strengthen the freedom to learn, teach, and research so that the American system of higher education can reclaim its mantle of best in the world,” Mike Gavin, CEO of the Alliance for Higher Education, said in a statement Wednesday. “The hope at the Alliance for Higher Education is that the new Congress will put a check on the current administration’s blatant attacks designed to keep working class Americans and people of color from accessing higher education and a better life.”

Reining in student debt is one of the specific issues some advocates want this new slate of Democratic lawmakers to address.

Aissa Canchola Bañez, policy director for the consumer protection group Protect Borrowers, said in a statement that the election results send “a strong message to the Trump Administration and lawmakers of both parties in Washington: lower costs and enact debt relief now for working families—not special interests.” The group, she added, is looking to Congress “to tackle the affordability and household debt crisis” and “hold the Trump Administration and the special interests that have capitalized on the financial desperation of working families accountable.”

The National College Attainment Network said it’s also interpreting Tuesday’s election as a signal that Americans want the government to make the costs of daily life—including education—more affordable.

“A college degree remains the most reliable route to a family-sustaining wage, but for too many students it is out of reach,” the group wrote in a LinkedIn post. “NCAN looks forward to working with members of Congress, governors, and state legislators to help drive economic mobility for students and families and economic growth for the country.”

—Kathryn Palmer

title: 3 Takeaways on Enrollment Management
summary:
3 Takeaways on Enrollment Management Johanna Alonso Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM The annual conference of enrollment “data nerds” took place this week in Baltimore. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso 3 Takeaways on Enrollment Management
Johanna Alonso Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM

The annual conference of enrollment “data nerds” took place this week in Baltimore.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
BALTIMORE—Strategic enrollment management is 50 years old.

The practice, by which institutions aim to reach their enrollment goals through a holistic focus on everything from recruitment to graduation, has become a key concept in higher education, especially as institutions navigate a tumultuous landscape rife with threats to their enrollments. Originally known simply as enrollment management, the strategy was first conceived in 1974 by Boston College’s then–executive vice president Frank Campanella in a memo at a perhaps equally difficult time: the post–baby boom enrollment crisis. (The term first appeared in print in 1976, which is why 2026 is considered SEM’s semicentennial.)

At the time, Campanella wrote that enrollment management would “shortly be the ‘name of the game.’” Attendees at this year’s Strategic Enrollment Management Conference would likely agree.

But SEM, as those in the field call it, has changed a lot in half a century. On display at the conference, which is organized each year by the American Association of Collegiate Registrars and Admissions Officers and was hosted at the Baltimore Marriott Waterfront, were new ideas about how to use artificial intelligence in enrollment management, fervent discussions of the so-called demographic cliff and deep dives into how institutions use data to inform enrollment decisions.

Melanie Gottlieb, AACRAO’s executive director, noted that of the association’s various convenings, the SEM conference is the one that attracts the most “data nerds.” AI has been exciting for the SEM community, she said, because it can make enrollment analysis more accessible to those without a traditional data background.

“There’s this balance between using AI to understand data or to drive automation on things so that there is more time and space for the human touch, which is really required in an enrollment space,” she said. “Students don’t want to be thought about as numbers.”

Other key themes included institutions’ efforts to attract nontraditional students, making enrollment seamless for students and the importance of retention in strategic enrollment management. Read on to learn more about Inside Higher Ed’s top takeaways from the conference, which wraps up today.

1. Nontraditional students take center stage

Many sessions focused on nontraditional students, from adult learners at large to veterans, as well as dual-enrollment students—high schoolers taking college courses—which is one of the fastest-growing enrollment sectors.

Institutions across the country are increasingly relying on students outside of the traditional secondary school pipeline to bolster enrollment, especially with high school graduation pools shrinking in some states. That means traditional enrollment management practices have to adapt, panelists from Indiana University said at a presentation about online students.

The panel, which highlighted the university’s growing online population, argued that traditional SEM is built on a “predictable student acquisition pathway” that follows the institution’s application and admission timeline. But online students, they argued, often juggle their education with paid work and families and need institutions to be responsive to their schedules. They don’t want to wait months after they apply to hear if they are admitted, said Whitnie Powell, IU Online’s assistant vice president of enrollment management and student services; when they apply, it’s often when they’re ready to get started.

The panelists also said that many online students don’t fit neatly into labels like “new student” or “continuing student.” Internal research at IU Online showed that about 11 percent of students were returning after having stopped out more than two years prior, and 86 percent of those previously stopped-out students had been in-person learners in the past. Those students may have needs that differ from those of their peers who started their degrees online, for instance, or who never took a break from school.

Another session, presented by Thomas Soule, associate director of learning evaluations for the American Council on Education, focused on credit for prior learning—including trainings and military experience—for military members. Soule noted that accepting these credits and ensuring CPL policies are clear and easy for prospective students to find can play a valuable role in attracting military learners.

2. An emphasis on ease

Speakers highlighted their institutions’ efforts to decrease friction for applicants, from simplifying scholarships through tuition promise programs to hiring new staff to help smooth the matriculation process for new students.

Danny Hodorowski, who has served as the new student liaison for the National University of Health Sciences since 2025, has one-on-one meetings with every single admitted student to ensure they don’t experience bumps in the enrollment process. He double-checks all of their files, ensures their background checks are completed, helps them arrange housing and more, with the goal of reducing summer melt.

“It’s a total onboarding experience for them before they get to campus,” he said.

Though he doesn’t yet have data on how the role has impacted yield, Hodorowski said during his presentation, he believes that the melt the university experienced this year mostly had to do with students’ personal circumstances rather than anything the university could have done differently.

In presentations about financial aid, speakers also emphasized the importance of clarity and straightforward language. That’s exemplified by a recent surge in tuition promise programs, in which colleges say they will cover all tuition for families below specific income thresholds. In most cases, that’s not a significant change in how the money is distributed, but more a shift in marketing: advertising “free tuition” makes sense to families, whereas industry jargon does not.

“Families do not know what ‘demonstrated unmet need’ is … it was so unclear and confusing that it really made no sense” to use that language, said Jay Goff, vice president and dean of enrollment management and student success at George Washington University. The institution launched its Revolutionary Promise for students with family incomes under $150,000 this fall.

IU’s presentation on online learners also pointed out places institutions can remove friction from the admissions process for those students, such as by limiting how many different offices they have to interface with. And Chris Foley, associate vice president for IU Online, took issue with the notion that students who want a seamless process are just lazy.

"[Students] are just like us, to tell you the truth. I wouldn’t spend more than five minutes to register for a Netflix account, but I’ll happily watch 16 hours of Stranger Things. I want good content; I don’t want [to be] struggling with friction,” he said.

3. Retention as enrollment management

Multiple speakers noted that recruiting new students is seen as the glitzy, attractive part of enrollment management. But retention—keeping recruits at the university from year to year—also plays a major role.

The importance of retention has sometimes been obscured by its place in the structure of a university. Historically, “everybody is responsible for retention, but no one is accountable” for it, said Stanley Henderson, retired vice chancellor for enrollment management and student life at the University of Michigan–Dearborn and AACRAO consultant emeritus, during a session on the history of SEM.

Kay Eilers, who leads the Division of Strategic Enrollment Management and Student Success at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, echoed that sentiment. Her institution recently launched a strategic enrollment plan featuring retention as one of its two pillars, and that work has involved making strategic enrollment a campuswide initiative that involves everyone from student life administrators to the faculty.

“When we hear about recruitment, there are people who are hired for that to be their primary role,” she said. “But it’s really about the environment that we’re creating … if the student doesn’t have a great experience in the classroom or in regards to student life, they might not stay.”

title: Helping Students Make It to Year 2
summary:
Helping Students Make It to Year 2 Joshua.Bay Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM Six Pennsylvania public universities are launching a program to aid first-generation and low-income students in building connections and persisting into their sophomore year. Byline(s) Joshua Bay Helping Students Make It to Year 2
Joshua.Bay Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM

Six Pennsylvania public universities are launching a program to aid first-generation and low-income students in building connections and persisting into their sophomore year.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
The transition between a student’s first and second years of college is often fraught with challenges, from understanding how to renew financial aid to navigating advising, course registration and campus life. For students who are the first in their families to attend college, that transition can be especially difficult.

To address these issues, six universities in Pennsylvania’s State System of Higher Education are launching a coordinated program to help first-generation and low-income students successfully transition from their first to second year of college.

The program, Mastering Academic and Professional Systems, or MAPS, will enroll 12 first-year students at each university—72 students in all—in a structured, yearlong initiative that includes monthly cohort meetings, faculty and staff mentoring, and financial aid guidance—including FAFSA renewal assistance—and experiential activities that connect students with campus resources.

Kalani Palmer, a professor of professional studies in education at Indiana University of Pennsylvania, who is leading the program, said student retention efforts often focus on the transition from the first to second semester, devoting less attention to the transition between the first and second years.

MAPS aims to fill that gap by reaching first-generation students who may not already be involved in campus life through activities such as athletics or Greek life, she said, helping them build social capital, develop a sense of belonging and better navigate university resources and support systems.

“University admissions teams do a lot to support students when they’re seniors in high school and coming in, but from year one to year two, you don’t get the same level of support,” Palmer said. “We’re trying to make sure that we’re catching the students that are not already well-connected and well-established by the end of their first year.”

Closing support gaps: The initiative comes as other universities are recognizing the importance of supporting students beyond their first year. At the University of Michigan, for example, the LSA First Fellows program connects first-generation sophomores with campus resources, mentors and opportunities, recognizing that institutional support can diminish after the first year even as students begin making important decisions about their majors, careers and involvement outside the classroom.

Palmer said MAPS originated from a project she was developing for the HERS Leadership Institute that focused on students at Indiana University of Pennsylvania. After she applied for funding from the Posner Foundation of Pittsburgh, the initiative expanded to six of the 14 universities in Pennsylvania’s public university system.

MAPS is funded by a $250,000, two-year grant from the philanthropic organization to the PASSHE Foundation, an independent philanthropic and strategic partner to the state’s public higher education system.

Although roughly 80 percent of PASSHE students return for their second year, retention rates are lower among students from low-income backgrounds. Among first-time, full-time students who entered in fall 2024, 75.2 percent of Pell Grant recipients returned for their second year, compared to 82.8 percent of students who did not receive Pell Grants, according to system data.

Palmer said MAPS aims to strengthen retention among low-income and first-generation students by providing additional support during their first year.

“The way the system operates really privileges people who have relationships and connections,” Palmer said. “Sometimes those students don’t have those relationships and connections, and they’re not aware of all of these different opportunities and resources that really can support them.”

“Challenges come for everyone in this population, so just giving them the tools and the support that they need to be able to navigate those challenges is important,” she added.

As part of the grant, officials will develop a training course for faculty and staff focused on making higher education more transparent, equitable and accessible. Participants will earn a certificate and digital badge upon completion, and the training is intended to serve as a lasting resource that can be offered and expanded to other institutions.

Palmer said the training will help faculty and staff better understand the hidden curriculum of higher education and their role in helping students navigate it. By encouraging employees across departments to build relationships, share information and connect students with resources, she hopes to foster a broader culture of student support rather than leave that responsibility to individual offices.

“Our state system does a lot to support students, but the students that need it don’t always see it or get it because of how we communicate that information or don’t communicate it,” Palmer said. “That’s the role the institution can play in being less siloed and more connected.”

Why this matters: As MAPS gets underway, Palmer said one measure of success will be whether faculty and staff work more collaboratively to ensure first-generation and low-income students receive the support they need.

“Sometimes they’re working on the same goals but not together so things get missed,” Palmer said. “Seeing those relationships between faculty and staff strengthened at each institution would be a sign of success.”

For students, Palmer said she will be monitoring retention and persistence from their first to second year, as well as their sense of belonging, connections with peers, involvement in campus activities and understanding of university support systems.

Ultimately, she hopes to identify which aspects of the program are effective and sustainable enough to be integrated into existing student support structures and expanded across all PASSHE universities.

“Their confidence around academics, their comfort with accessing resources, their feeling of belonging,” she said. “Finding out how we can take the things that work well in this project and embed them into our existing structure and spread it across our state system would be the most ideal for me.”

title: From Sage on the Stage to Steward of the Struggle
summary:
From Sage on the Stage to Steward of the Struggle  Elizabeth Redden Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM The rise of generative AI has changed the faculty member’s role. Byline(s) Inara Scott From Sage on the Stage to Steward of the Struggle 
Elizabeth Redden Wed, 11/04/2026 - 03:00 AM

The rise of generative AI has changed the faculty member’s role.

Byline(s)
Inara Scott
full_text:
For many years, experts in teaching and learning have leaned into the idea that a higher education faculty member’s job has—or should have—moved from the “sage on the stage” to the “guide on the side.” This shift represented a change from lecture-based teaching, where the faculty member stands in front of a class and provides content, to active teaching, where the faculty member facilitates student engagement, often in a flipped-classroom environment where students engage directly with course materials and the faculty member facilitates their learning experience. In the “guide on the side” experience, the faculty member might physically move around a classroom as students work on problems, answering questions or stepping in when students get stuck or need redirection.

In both cases, past students generally had two choices when it came to completing their work: doing it themselves, or having another human do it for them. While some specific tasks could be completed by word processors or calculators, if a faculty member received an assignment from a student, it generally reflected that student’s effort (or blatant cheating).

Today, thanks to artificial intelligence and tools like ChatGPT, students have endless options when it comes to what they complete on their own and what type of assistance they receive from AI. That means our work as faculty has changed. Our most important role is no longer as a guide who answers questions and facilitates assignment completion, nor is it as a provider of content. The computers in our pockets can do these things quite handily. Instead, today’s faculty must guide students to the useful cognitive struggle that is at the essence of their class, creating experiences and designing assignments that further cognitive agency and durable learning.

From Sage on the Stage to Steward of the Struggle

What does it mean to be the steward of the struggle? It means identifying for students where the productive and important cognitive friction resides in the class and what tasks they can safely offload to technology. It means identifying for students what they should be able to do on their own, independent of technology, where it is permissible to use technology as an aid or scaffold and what they can delegate altogether.

It means identifying what work must remain solely human and what can be aided by technology.

Some may want to argue it must all remain human. Students should be able to do everything without AI. This position misunderstands the notions of cognitive offloading and cognitive load theory. Cognitive offloading is not an enemy of learning. Cognitive load theory recognizes that humans have limited working memory, so effective course design includes offloading unimportant tasks while focusing working memory and effort on essential learning outcomes. If my learning outcomes are related to creating and solving algebraic problems, I may permit the use of calculators for basic calculations because offloading that routine task allows the student to focus on the more complex cognitive challenge. Or if I am teaching students to develop persuasive arguments, I may allow the use of word processors to check and fix spelling, punctuation and grammar.

The challenge for today’s faculty is to draw those lines and effectively communicate them to students:

Yes, you can use AI to help you find the elements of a tort, but you must be able to recall the basic concept of the tort without AI assistance so you can recognize it in a business scenario.

Yes, you can use AI to draft lovely prose, but you cannot use it to develop a persuasive argument structure for a debate.

Yes, AI can tell you the formula for straight-line depreciation, but you must recognize the need for that type of accounting without being prompted by AI.

These lines will likely be different when a student is in fourth grade (no calculators allowed) and in graduate school (use all the calculators you want). They will also reflect the discipline at issue (no spelling help from technology in a language class; use all you want in a physics class).

To be clear, these are hypotheticals, not meant to apply to your class or your discipline. That’s the point. Only you know where the line is for you and what you need your students to be able to accomplish.

Teaching this way will require us to entirely rethink our learning outcomes (“What can a student do as a result of this class?”). Today, students can do anything, with or without our classes … with the help of AI. That means the question today is: What can a student do without any assistance from AI, and what can they do with assistance? What must remain in their brain, so they can carry it around to a meeting or a worksite, and what can they develop in more detail later, with assistance from AI? What do we want to protect as a core unassisted human skill and what are we comfortable seeing offloaded to or aided by technology?

Being the steward of the struggle also means understanding that learning requires friction. Learning theory and psychology have long identified pathways to durable learning, and they require desirable difficulty, generating things rather than reviewing them and techniques like retrieval practice and interleaving. As faculty, these are tools we must now employ, and we must do so deliberately and transparently.

In my ethics class, I ask students to generate summaries of cases on their own, unassisted by technology, and then work with AI as a Socratic dialogue partner to test their understanding of the core dilemma. I ask them to identify ethical pitfalls and develop strategies to structure more ethical workplaces without the use of AI and then permit the use of AI to refine, test and further develop specific plans. While they do generate polished memorandums, the final work product is a relatively small portion of their grade. I allow the use of AI to polish their writing and organization because I have broken out the hard work in scaffolded steps throughout the term and seen evidence of the unassisted and assisted AI work in various other forms.

Faculty may be frustrated by students’ overreliance on AI, but let’s be clear: Without a road map, students don’t know what aspects of the intellectual struggle they should retain. I have seen students waste hours rereading notes that were drafted by AI; they did not know that it was the generation of the notes that would have resulted in durable learning. I have seen students use AI to outline an argument, sometimes with the knowledge of their professor, without realizing that they would be less able to create their own arguments in the future. And I have seen students spend hours memorizing formulas or four-part tests that they would immediately forget two months later, rather than focusing on durable understanding of an underlying concept that we would have wanted them to retain.

As stewards of the struggle, we have a deep responsibility to identify for our students key cognitive processes and the classification of the knowledge and skills we are including in our classes. We need to tell our students where the cognitive struggle should reside and where it can be delegated. We have a new job, and it’s time we started doing it.

title: The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
summary: For some young Africans, these victories offer a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could do at home.
full_text:
"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".

It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.

Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.

The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.

"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.

El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.

The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.

But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.

The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.

At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.

Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.

Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.

Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.

Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.

She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.

Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".

She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.

Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.

The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.

Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.

His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.

In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.

Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.

First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.

Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.

Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.

Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.

Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.

For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.

On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

title: Crises have taken their classrooms. But education cannot wait
summary: "Today, the education of 258 million school-aged children worldwide is disrupted by crises," says Reem Alabali Radovan, Germany's Minister for Development in an exclusive op-ed for Euronews. That is why Germany is providing €20 million in funding for education in emergencies over the coming years.
full_text:
In the flood-swept valleys of Nepal, children are sleeping in the very classrooms where they used to learn. In Sudan, more than five thousand schools stand closed, leaving an entire generation waiting for peace.

In Ukraine, in Gaza, in the Sahel, children caught in the world's conflicts ask for remarkably little: a classroom, a teacher, a desk. Today, the education of 258 million school-aged children worldwide is disrupted by crises. For these children, missing out on quality education means missing out on chances in life.

Global spending on education aid could fall by 24 per cent this year

Meanwhile, the aid the world provides for education is projected to fall by 24 per cent this year. In the very emergencies where education matters most, it is being neglected. This is a political failure before it is a financial one.

With major consequences: When we fail to educate children in crises, we do not merely postpone their futures – we mortgage our own. Children that are denied learning are more vulnerable to violence, recruitment into armed groups, exploitation and early marriage.

Girls are often the first to be denied access to education – and the last to return to school. And the societies that lose a generation to illiteracy do not quietly disappear; they export instability, forced displacement and conflict across borders. Excluding children from school today will deepen the security, economic and social challenges of tomorrow. In the short term, school is the most effective lifeline for children.

A classroom is a place of safety, of meals, of psychosocial support, of normality in the abnormal. Getting children back to learning within days of a disaster is the difference between trauma and recovery – and it is also the difference between hope and the loss of it.

The global fund for education in emergencies is very important

In the long term, school is the most effective development policy there is. It is essential for peace and stability. Every additional year of education makes a lasting difference: for literacy, for livelihoods, for girls who marry later and lead sooner, for teachers who train the next generation, for communities that can absorb a flood or a war and rebuild.

That is why the work of Education Cannot Wait (ECW), the global fund for education in emergencies, is so important. Over a decade of action, ECW and its partners have enabled education for more than 16 million crisis-affected children across 33,000 schools, even in the toughest places.

Nearly 300.000 teachers – over half of them women – have been trained. And ECW has an ambitious goal: to improve access to education for another 10 million of the world's most crisis-affected children over the next four years.

As an international community, we can make it happen if we all contribute. That is why, at a time when others are stepping back from multilateralism, Germany is stepping forward. We have committed €20 million per year to ECW for 2027-2031 – contributing to its US$600 million replenishment target.

Germany is sending a clear message

Knowing that budgets are tight, we make this commitment with open eyes. Because the evidence is unambiguous: there is no more effective way to build peace, no faster way to restore dignity, and no smarter investment in our own security than a child in a classroom.

With this commitment, Germany is sending a clear message: we strongly believe in multilateral partnerships. And we remain a reliable partner. Only through collective action can we find solutions to global challenges and ensure stability worldwide. Now we ask our partners in the G7, in Europe and beyond to do the same.

We must not let education become the silent casualty of our times. Together, we can make a difference – so that every child, everywhere, has the chance to learn and build a better future.

title: International universities face pressure to prove value in India
summary:
At AIEC, delegates said universities will need to match international credentials with local career pathways, mobility and credible partnerships.

The post International universities face pressure to prove value in India appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
International universities expanding in India must go beyond global branding and regulatory approvals to build credible career pathways, mobility options and trusted local partnerships, delegates heard at Australian International Education Conference (AIEC) 2026.

“India is ready for TNE. India wants TNE,” said Vik Singh, trade and investment commissioner for Austrade in South Asia.

The challenge, speakers suggested, is whether overseas institutions are ready for India’s price-sensitive, employment-focused and operationally complex market.

The discussion formed part of Bringing global campuses to India: is the market really ready for TNE?, chaired by Steve Berridge, CEO of ECA Ventures.

The panel included Lawrence Pratchett, inaugural provost of Birkbeck, University of London’s Bengaluru campus and chief executive of UniReady Global; Caryn Nery, director of transnational education partnerships at Victoria University and IEAA TNE Network convener; and Singh.

The question is becoming increasingly urgent as overseas providers turn approvals into operating campuses.

The University of Liverpool has welcomed nearly 300 students to its Bengaluru campus, while the University of Western Australia has opened in Mumbai and secured approval for a Chennai campus.

The University of Colorado Denver is also planning to begin teaching in Hyderabad in 2027, subject to final University Grants Commission (UGC) approval, while Telangana is developing a Future City policy to attract overseas institutions.

Flinders University has announced plans for a Bengaluru campus, reflecting India’s growing importance to Australia’s education relationship as the latter’s onshore visa settings become more restrictive.

Yet the first wave of expansion has not settled whether international campuses can build a durable market.

Research by Rahul Choudaha, previously reported by The PIE, mapped 13 international universities admitting students across 14 Indian campuses in 2026/27, with modest initial cohorts and limited graduate-outcome data encouraging a wait-and-watch approach among families.

The research found that first-year undergraduate fees at the campuses examined were, on average, 115% higher than at selected leading Indian private universities, although they were around 36% of fees at their overseas parent campuses before scholarships.

India doesn’t want a scattering of MOUs that hang on the wall. It’s deeper partnerships that deliver

Vik Singh, Austrade

For Berridge, the sector is still waiting for proof of success at scale. He told delegates there were not yet “case studies of at-scale success” for international branch campuses in India.

For Pratchett, the policy opening has created opportunity, but not certainty. “The policy environment is quite fluid,” he said.

He said the UGC’s framework was stable at a high level, but that providers still had to navigate changing expectations around subjects, international faculty and delivery models.

Pratchett said the regulator appeared more interested in STEM provision than humanities and social sciences, while Singh highlighted unresolved questions around online learning, work-integrated learning and the treatment of international institutions within India’s higher education system.

Singh said state policy would shape the sector’s next phase, with providers needing to consider local incentives, infrastructure, tax treatment, commuting patterns and families’ purchasing power in each city.

That aligns with the wider push by states such as Telangana, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh to position international campuses within technology, research and urban-development strategies.

But a more open policy environment alone will not create demand.

“I’m not competing with UNSW or Liverpool down the road from me,” Pratchett said. “I’m competing with the local universities.”

That means international providers need to explain why their offer is different from a well-established Indian private university with local brand recognition, alumni networks and visible employer relationships.

An Emeritus survey published in October found that 68% of respondents were likely or extremely likely to consider a program offered in India by an international university.

However, interest does not establish willingness or ability to pay, particularly as a weaker rupee, rising overseas tuition and living costs, and uncertainty around immigration rules force families to examine the likely return on their investment more closely.

The attraction of an international qualification at home is also not simply about avoiding overseas study.

Oxford International’s latest mobility survey found that 81% of surveyed Indian study-abroad aspirants expected to return home after graduation, suggesting students can value global exposure while intending to build their careers in India.

Nery said aspirational TNE students often wanted an opportunity to study at their university’s home campus, whether through a semester abroad, transfer route or other form of mobility.

That expectation has become harder to meet as visa restrictions tighten in major destinations, she said, leaving universities to ensure their India-based offer has value in its own right.

The panel’s clearest consensus was that career outcomes would be decisive.

“There is a difference between employability and employment,” Singh said. “Employment is not the answer. Employability is the answer.”

He said university rankings could open doors, but families ultimately wanted to know which employers would hire graduates and what salaries they could expect.

Singh said Australian companies operating in India could help build talent pipelines, while universities needed to embed internships, work-integrated learning, career guidance and employer engagement from the beginning.

At Birkbeck Bengaluru, Pratchett said the university was involving employers through course advisory boards and engaging local venture capitalists to help students understand the city’s startup ecosystem.

The aim, he said, was to make students think about careers and the skills required for them from the start of their studies, rather than only when they began applying for jobs.

The discussion also underlined that a branch campus is only one route into India.

Nery pointed to models including the RMIT–BITS Pilani partnership and online postgraduate programs as examples of the range of options available to institutions.

The panel heard that, despite varying capital risk and mobility options, all models depend on local knowledge, credible partners and a clear proposition for students.

For Singh, the lesson was that expansion cannot be built on symbolic agreements alone. “India doesn’t want a scattering of MoUs that hang on the wall,” he said. “It’s deeper partnerships that deliver.”

title: Beyond academic support: why mentoring matters for international students
summary:
International students cross not only geographical borders when they come to study abroad, but also an academic one. Echos Education's Aysat Orujova explains why mentoring matters for international students.

The post Beyond academic support: why mentoring matters for international students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The realisation that everything you have ever known is completely unreliable can be crushing.

Growing up in a system with its own rigid rules is challenging enough. Being told that, actually, none of that fits here and you better figure it out before the end of next week can be nothing short of an absolute nightmare.

Yet, that is the reality for many international students. Arriving in the UK, with an impressive academic record and a shining diploma to prove it, students are quick to realise that they did not just cross geographical borders, but also an academic one.

This puts them in quite a precarious position. The period meant to be exciting and lively, begins to feel extremely isolating, leaving many students with what we call an ‘academic paralysis.’

Overwhelmed by unfamiliar responsibilities and the quickly piling assignments, students find it more accessible to convince themselves that they are simply incapable of producing quality work. It becomes easier to hide from the danger, which sometimes takes the form of parents and teachers seeking answers.

Before approaching international students, we have to acknowledge how different academic expectations are across the world. Students grow up with different goalposts, which they work towards their entire academic lives. Countries that focus on rote learning are more likely to produce candidates who did not get a chance to develop their critical thinking, research and writing skills, all of which are vital parts of the UK education.

Hence when students arrive in the UK with good grades but without the correct expectations, they can be caught off guard by how behind they are from the rest of the class.

In our view, the point of mentoring is to address such gaps in knowledge with a more familiar approach. At Echos, mentoring has helped us develop a connection with our students beyond the application stages.

Almost all of them struggle with unlearning old habits and adapting to a more independent environment. Structuring a study programme around their individual needs, providing frequent feedback and being there for them more as a study companion than just an authority figure, gives them the space to learn how to balance their responsibilities, grow in confidence and still feel like they have a community they can rely on.

Last year, when a student who at first only met the minimum level subject requirement graduated top of his foundation class we knew we had achieved something that was quite meaningful.

International students have much to offer to academic settings.

They are bright thinkers with unique backgrounds and experiences, qualities that have and will always be a valuable asset for any institution. Which is why we believe that introducing mentoring into the routines of international students gives them the platform to realise their full potential.

It is effective because it goes beyond the expected subject support. It offers them a support system and the reassurance that they are not alone in this journey.

About the author:

Aysat Orujova is an education consultant and mentor coordinator at Echos Education. She provides consultancy services on UK’s university applications, as well as mentoring students in academic and creative writing. She has a BA in History and International Relations from King’s College London and an MA in Creative Writing from Royal Holloway.

title: L’università si svuota. E non è colpa degli studenti
summary: Se l’ateneo diventa un luogo dove superare esami, cercare la strada più rapida è razionale. Per cambiare le abitudini di studio servono università in cui valga la pena stare. Ci lamentiamo perché gli studenti leggono sempre meno manuali e preparano gli esami soprattutto con slide, appunti e riassunti. Un’indagine realizzata da Talents Venture per l’Associazione […]
full_text:
Se l’ateneo diventa un luogo dove superare esami, cercare la strada più rapida è razionale. Per cambiare le abitudini di studio servono università in cui valga la pena stare.

Ci lamentiamo perché gli studenti leggono sempre meno manuali e preparano gli esami soprattutto con slide, appunti e riassunti. Un’indagine realizzata da Talents Venture per l’Associazione Italiana Editori, che ha coinvolto 463 docenti di 34 atenei, registra una preoccupazione diffusa per la preparazione degli studenti. È la percezione dei professori, non una misurazione diretta di quanto gli studenti imparino. Ma solleva una domanda importante: che università abbiamo costruito intorno a loro?

Ci lamentiamo perché gli studenti trattano l’università come un luogo dove sostenere esami. Eppure abbiamo progressivamente costruito un sistema che li incentiva a viverla proprio così. Se il traguardo è superare una prova, prepararsi sulle slide può essere una scelta razionale: permette di concentrarsi sugli argomenti essenziali e passare più rapidamente all’esame successivo. Non significa necessariamente imparare altrettanto. Significa rispondere a un percorso scandito da crediti da accumulare, prove da superare e tempi di laurea da rispettare.

C’è però un aspetto di cui parliamo meno: le nostre università sono luoghi nei quali è piacevole trascorrere il proprio tempo? In molte sedi gli spazi sono organizzati soprattutto intorno alle attività programmate: aule per le lezioni, corridoi per spostarsi, biblioteche spesso affollate. Non sempre ci sono ambienti accoglienti nei quali fermarsi a studiare, discutere o incontrare altre persone. Esistono naturalmente atenei e dipartimenti che hanno investito molto in questa direzione. Ma se l’università offre poche occasioni di vita condivisa al di fuori delle attività obbligatorie, è comprensibile che venga frequentata soprattutto per quelle.

Una riflessione analoga riguarda i docenti. La presenza quotidiana nei dipartimenti è condizionata da fattori organizzativi e logistici: la distanza tra casa e lavoro, gli impegni didattici e amministrativi, il tempo da dedicare alla ricerca. E non tutti i dipartimenti offrono spazi e occasioni di confronto che rendano naturale trascorrervi l’intera giornata. Non è una questione di scarso impegno individuale, ma di condizioni che possono ridurre le opportunità di vivere l’università come comunità.

Lo studente intermittente e il professore intermittente producono così un’università intermittente: un luogo che tutti attraversano, ma che sempre meno persone abitano davvero. Eppure un ateneo dovrebbe essere molto più di un posto nel quale qualcuno tiene lezioni e qualcun altro sostiene esami. Dovrebbe permettere a persone con competenze e curiosità differenti di trascorrere abbastanza tempo insieme da far nascere idee impreviste.

Uno studente che si ferma a parlare con un professore, due ricercatori che scoprono davanti a un caffè di occuparsi dello stesso problema, un seminario seguito semplicemente perché interessante: sono momenti che non assegnano crediti e difficilmente entrano negli indicatori di valutazione. Eppure fanno parte della formazione e della produzione di conoscenza. Se studenti e docenti si incontrano quasi soltanto per attività programmate, queste occasioni si rarefanno.

Per questo la qualità degli spazi non è un lusso estetico. Biblioteche luminose, cortili, giardini, caffetterie, sale comuni e luoghi nei quali studiare e lavorare insieme sono infrastrutture della conoscenza. Non servono campus da cartolina: servono ambienti che offrano buone ragioni per rimanere anche quando non c’è nulla di obbligatorio da fare. Investirvi significa investire nelle relazioni che rendono possibile imparare e fare ricerca.

La crescita delle università telematiche rende ancora più evidente la questione. Se un ateneo tradizionale viene percepito soltanto come un servizio che offre lezioni, materiali ed esami, l’online può risultare più flessibile. L’università in presenza dovrebbe valorizzare ciò che uno schermo difficilmente sostituisce: la condivisione quotidiana di spazi, esperienze e relazioni.

Torniamo allora alle slide e ai manuali. Il punto non è solo quali materiali scelgano gli studenti, ma che significato attribuiscano all’esperienza universitaria. Quando l’ateneo diventa una successione di prove da superare, cercare il modo più efficiente per farlo è comprensibile. Se desideriamo un rapporto più profondo con lo studio, dobbiamo offrire a studenti e professori qualcosa di più di un calendario di obblighi: un’università nella quale valga la pena restare.

Eppure un ateneo dovrebbe essere molto più di un posto nel quale qualcuno tiene lezioni e qualcun altro sostiene esami. Dovrebbe permettere a persone con competenze e curiosità differenti di trascorrere abbastanza tempo insieme da far nascere idee impreviste.

Uno studente che si ferma a parlare con un professore, due ricercatori che scoprono davanti a un caffè di occuparsi dello stesso problema, un seminario seguito semplicemente perché interessante: sono momenti che non assegnano crediti e difficilmente entrano negli indicatori di valutazione. Eppure fanno parte della formazione e della produzione di conoscenza. Se studenti e docenti si incontrano quasi soltanto per attività programmate, queste occasioni si rarefanno.

Per questo la qualità degli spazi non è un lusso estetico. Biblioteche luminose, cortili, giardini, caffetterie, sale comuni e luoghi nei quali studiare e lavorare insieme sono infrastrutture della conoscenza. Non servono campus da cartolina: servono ambienti che offrano buone ragioni per rimanere anche quando non c’è nulla di obbligatorio da fare. Investirvi significa investire nelle relazioni che rendono possibile imparare e fare ricerca.

La crescita delle università telematiche rende ancora più evidente la questione. Se un ateneo tradizionale viene percepito soltanto come un servizio che offre lezioni, materiali ed esami, l’online può risultare più flessibile. L’università in presenza dovrebbe valorizzare ciò che uno schermo difficilmente sostituisce: la condivisione quotidiana di spazi, esperienze e relazioni.

Torniamo allora alle slide e ai manuali. Il punto non è solo quali materiali scelgano gli studenti, ma che significato attribuiscano all’esperienza universitaria. Quando l’ateneo diventa una successione di prove da superare, cercare il modo più efficiente per farlo è comprensibile. Se desideriamo un rapporto più profondo con lo studio, dobbiamo offrire a studenti e professori qualcosa di più di un calendario di obblighi: un’università nella quale valga la pena restare.

title: Liceo matematico, la vera sfida è insegnare a pensare
summary:
Il Liceo matematico affianca formule e calcolo a storia delle idee, creatività e connessioni interdisciplinari. Un approccio che acquista peso nell’era dell’intelligenza artificiale

L'articolo Liceo matematico, la vera sfida è insegnare a pensare proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
In Italia, la recente introduzione sperimentale del Liceo matematico rappresenta un segnale importante. L’obiettivo non è semplicemente aumentare il numero di ore dedicate alla materia, ma sviluppare le capacità di ragionamento e di risoluzione dei problemi, creando anche collegamenti con discipline che possono sembrare lontane. È una direzione che trovo particolarmente interessante, perché invita a ripensare non tanto che cosa insegniamo, quanto il significato che attribuiamo all’insegnamento della matematica.

La matematica nella vita quotidiana e il valore del ragionamento

La matematica ha ancora troppo spesso la reputazione di essere una disciplina astratta, austera, riservata a chi possiede un talento particolare. Eppure, è presente continuamente nella nostra vita, anche dove meno ce lo aspettiamo. Quando leggiamo un sondaggio e cerchiamo di capire che cosa significhi il margine di errore, quando ci interroghiamo sull’attendibilità di una statistica vista sui social network o quando un’applicazione calcola il percorso più rapido per tornare a casa, stiamo entrando, in modi diversi, nel territorio della matematica. Persino durante una partita di calcio la matematica non è mai troppo lontana: dietro la traiettoria di un tiro entrano in gioco geometria e fisica, mentre le strategie di un portiere e di un attaccante durante un calcio di rigore possono essere analizzate attraverso la teoria dei giochi. Probabilità, statistica, geometria, algoritmi e ottimizzazione non sono soltanto nozioni che troviamo nei manuali scolastici: sono strumenti attraverso i quali interpretiamo la realtà.

Ma la sua utilità va ben oltre la capacità di effettuare calcoli. La matematica ci insegna soprattutto a pensare. Di fronte a un problema, ci abitua a definire con chiarezza la domanda, individuare le informazioni pertinenti, distinguere ciò che sappiamo da ciò che non sappiamo, formulare ipotesi, procedere passo dopo passo e verificare le nostre conclusioni. Jordan Ellenberg ha definito la matematica «il prolungamento del buon senso attraverso altri mezzi». Una definizione che apprezzo particolarmente: fare matematica significa sviluppare abitudini intellettuali che possono accompagnarci ben oltre l’aula.

Liceo matematico: dare significato all’insegnamento

Per questo credo sia necessario far evolvere il modo in cui la insegniamo. I fondamentali restano indispensabili: non si può ragionare liberamente senza una certa padronanza del calcolo, dell’algebra o della geometria. Il problema nasce quando l’apprendimento degli strumenti diventa il fine stesso dell’insegnamento. Troppo spesso presentiamo agli studenti un metodo prima ancora di mostrare loro la domanda a cui risponde e il problema che permette di affrontare, sia che si tratti di misurare un rischio, di comprendere le crescite esponenziali o ancora di valutare l’attendibilità di una statistica. Insegnare un metodo senza spiegarne lo scopo è un po’ come consegnare una mappa senza indicare quale viaggio si debba compiere.

Restituire significato alla matematica vuol dire anche mostrarne la dimensione storica, culturale e creativa. Ogni concetto nasce da una domanda, da una necessità o da una volontà di comprendere meglio il mondo. Conoscere il contesto in cui sono nate e si sono sviluppate determinate idee permette agli studenti di vedere la matematica non come una costruzione immobile e già compiuta, ma come il risultato di intuizioni, tentativi, errori, dibattiti e scoperte.

È proprio per questo che considero promettente un approccio interdisciplinare come quello proposto dal Liceo matematico italiano. Studiare la geometria tridimensionale attraverso gli origami o mettere in relazione la matematica con la letteratura significa aprire nuove porte d’ingresso verso questa disciplina. La matematica non vive isolata dalle altre forme di conoscenza. La ritroviamo nella prospettiva della pittura rinascimentale, nelle strutture e nelle proporzioni della musica, nell’architettura, nella filosofia e nelle scienze sociali. Creare ponti tra questi ambiti non significa indebolire il rigore matematico, ma mostrare agli studenti che osservare, dedurre, riconoscere strutture, stabilire connessioni e passare all’astrazione sono altrettanti modi di interrogare la realtà.

Insegnare matematica nell’era dell’intelligenza artificiale

Questa capacità diventa ancora più importante con la diffusione dell’intelligenza artificiale. Le macchine possono già svolgere calcoli complessi e produrre risposte con una rapidità che nessun essere umano può eguagliare. Ma abbiamo già vissuto trasformazioni simili con le calcolatrici e con i computer, e non per questo abbiamo smesso di insegnare matematica. La tecnologia sposta piuttosto il valore di ciò che dobbiamo imparare. Se un sistema di intelligenza artificiale ci fornisce una risposta, dobbiamo essere in grado di stabilire se è corretta, plausibile o completamente assurda. La formulazione dei problemi, la scelta delle ipotesi, l’interpretazione dei risultati e la capacità di decidere che cosa farne diventano quindi ancora più importanti.

In quindici anni di insegnamento ho osservato studenti sempre più rapidi nel cercare informazioni, trovare una pista e arrivare a una risposta. È una capacità preziosa. Allo stesso tempo, noto quanto possa essere difficile mantenere a lungo l’attenzione su un problema che non offre immediatamente una soluzione. Mi piace descrivere questa evoluzione dicendo che gli studenti sono progressivamente passati dall’essere corridori di fondo a velocisti. Abbiamo però bisogno di entrambe le qualità. La rapidità e la capacità di adattamento sono punti di forza, ma alcuni problemi richiedono tempo, concentrazione e la capacità di accettare di non ottenere subito una risposta.

La matematica può allenare proprio questa forma di pazienza intellettuale. Ci insegna che sbagliare non significa interrompere il percorso e che cercare è parte integrante del processo. Nei libri di testo vediamo spesso soltanto il risultato finale, ordinato e coerente; la matematica reale, invece, si è sviluppata attraverso intuizioni, tentativi, errori e correzioni. Lasciare più spazio all’esplorazione e alla discussione può aiutare gli studenti a capire che fare matematica non significa recitare la risposta giusta, ma imparare a cercarla.

La matematica come strumento per comprendere il mondo

C’è infine una dimensione che riguarda tutti noi come cittadini. Saper leggere un dato, mettere in discussione un’affermazione, riconoscere un ordine di grandezza e cambiare idea quando i fatti dimostrano che abbiamo torto sono competenze essenziali. Più le risposte diventano immediate e facilmente accessibili, più acquista valore la capacità di valutarle criticamente. Il pensiero logico non ci fornisce automaticamente tutte le risposte, ma ci offre gli strumenti per porre domande migliori e non accettare necessariamente la soluzione più semplice o immediata.

La sperimentazione del Liceo matematico può quindi essere un’occasione preziosa per ripensare il modo in cui gli studenti scoprono questa disciplina. Le formule e le tecniche continueranno a essere necessarie, ma dovranno essere accompagnate dalle domande, dalla storia delle idee, dai collegamenti con altre discipline e dalla possibilità di esplorare. Il vero obiettivo non dovrebbe essere soltanto formare studenti capaci di risolvere un’equazione, ma persone capaci di affrontare un problema, comprenderne i presupposti, valutare le diverse opzioni e prendere una decisione ragionata.

Se riusciremo a riportare il ragionamento al centro dell’insegnamento, la matematica potrà tornare a essere ciò che è sempre stata: non soltanto una materia scolastica, ma anche uno strumento per comprendere il mondo e imparare a pensare.
